subsection: 6. The clothing and textile industries in Ireland

notes.h: Structure of the Irish clothing and textile industries
notes.b: The clothing and textile industries cover the design, manufacture, distribution and sale of clothing, textiles and accessories. Each stage passes the product on towards the consumer, and the whole sector is market-driven, so it depends on skill, imagination and creativity to keep up with what customers want.
points: The parts of the industry are designers, who create ranges (collections of garments), manufacturers of clothing and of textiles, distributors, and retailers such as shops, department stores and online sellers.
Manufacturers produce menswear, womenswear, children's wear, knitwear, sportswear, accessories, lingerie and footwear, so the industry covers almost everything people wear.
Designers create ranges that are made by manufacturers and sold through their own shops or through retailers.
Distributors and retailers move the finished goods from the factory to the consumer, through shops, department stores and online sales.
The industries provide employment in manufacture, distribution and sales, and they earn export income because Irish designers sell their work abroad.
Irish designers sell under their own label and also produce ranges for high street stores, which gives their designs a much wider customer base.

Local Enterprise Offices (the county and city enterprise support bodies that replaced the Enterprise Boards in 2014) give small firms and designers advice, training and grants, so they can grow their businesses.
notes.tip: Exams that ask about the industry's contribution want employment in manufacture, distribution and sales, export of the products listed, and promotion of Irish design. When naming the support body, give Local Enterprise Offices, the current name for the old Enterprise Boards.

notes.b: A cottage or home-based industry is a business run in or near a person's home, often by one or a few people making a product by hand and selling to craft shops or directly to customers. Small firms like these are especially important in rural areas.
points: Start-up costs are low, so a business can be set up without a large investment in premises or machinery.
The work can be fitted around family life, which suits people who cannot work fixed hours.
Cottage industries provide employment in rural areas and so help keep people in their communities.
Some work is subcontracted (given out by a larger business) to local people who do it at home, for example Aran knitting.
They keep traditional skills and crafts alive, such as hand-knitting, weaving, lace-making and crochet.
Small businesses can develop distinctive products that stand out from mass-produced clothing, and a successful one can grow into a larger business.
Hobbies can turn into businesses, especially when the economy is poor and people look for another source of income.
Cottage industries are often promoted through craft shops and design centres, which sell the work of makers directly to the public.
Their weaknesses are small scale, limited marketing and finance, and an income that can be low.
notes.tip: When asked for the role of small businesses and cottage industries, give rural employment, work done at home, subcontracting, low start-up cost and traditional skills.

notes.h: Why textile craft work is growing in popularity
notes.b: Knitting, stitching and similar crafts have become popular again. Several different reasons explain why, and an exam answer needs a few of them.
points: Socialising: people join knitting and stitching clubs to meet others.
Learning traditional skills, which many people want to pass on or take up for the first time.
Saving money, because making or mending an item yourself can cost less than buying it.
More free time, which gives people the chance to take up a craft.
Start-up businesses, because a craft can be turned into a small business with little money.
A desire for original items that are not mass-produced.
The social influence of celebrities who knit or wear handmade items.
notes.tip: For the reasons textile craft work is growing in popularity, give socialising, new skills, saving money, free time, start-up business and originality.

notes.b: Irish designers draw on traditional crafts for ideas and materials. This links modern fashion to Irish heritage and gives Irish design a recognisable identity.
points: Hand-knitting and hand-weaving inspire coats and coatigans (a long knitted jacket) that use Aran stitches, the textured stitches of Aran knitting.
Irish linen, woven from flax, is used for products ranging from light tops and skirts to heavy coats and jackets.
Lace and crochet work feature in wedding dresses and other occasion wear.
Hand-weaving produces textured fabrics that designers use in contemporary clothing.
Tweed, Aran sweaters and hand-weaving are recognised Irish products that link design to Irish heritage.
These traditional crafts contribute to the identity of Irish design, which designers use to market Irish fashion abroad.
John Rocha used Irish fabrics and Celtic influence to create unique designs.
notes.tip: For how traditional crafts influence Irish design, name Aran-stitch coats, linen from light tops to heavy coats, and lace and crochet in wedding dresses and occasion wear.

notes.b: Irish designers show that fashion can be a successful business in Ireland. Learn one or two designers well enough to name them and give two or three points about their work.
points: John Rocha and Simone Rocha are Irish designers whose work is sold internationally, and John Rocha uses Irish fabrics and Celtic influence in his designs.
Philip Treacy is a contemporary Irish milliner (hat designer) from Ahascragh, County Galway, known internationally for couture hats.

Philip Treacy studied fashion at NCAD in Dublin, then took a master's degree in millinery at the Royal College of Art in London, and he built an international career creating hats for couture, royalty and celebrities.
Lainey Keogh is known for knitwear, and Louise Kennedy is known for detailed work and designed for a previous president.
Other Irish designers include Paul Costelloe, Carolyn Donnelly, Sybil Connolly and Orla Kiely, who is Irish-born.
Irish designers have created clothing and accessories for royalty, celebrities, world leaders and major events.

Designers contribute to the industry by creating employment in manufacture, distribution and sales, exporting menswear, womenswear, children's wear, knitwear and accessories, and promoting Irish design at home and abroad.
notes.tip: When asked to name a designer and outline their work, name the designer first, then give two or three points: clothing and accessories for royalty, celebrities or events, employment, export, and promoting Irish design. John Rocha (Irish fabrics, Celtic designs) and Philip Treacy (millinery, international clients) are easy to write about.

notes.b: Irish fashion needs publicity and support to reach customers at home and abroad. Several routes help a designer or maker become known.
points: Local Enterprise Offices support small designers and makers with advice, training and grants.
Shops and design centres sell Irish design, for example Kilkenny Design Centre, a craft and design centre in Castle Yard, Kilkenny.
Designers produce ranges for high street stores, so their work reaches a wide public.
Irish designers show their collections at fashion weeks and international fashion shows, which gives them exposure to buyers and the press.
Press coverage and public figures wearing Irish designers' clothing create publicity for the designers.
Fashion blogs and social media promote Irish designers to a wide audience at home and abroad.
notes.tip: For how Irish fashion is promoted, give Local Enterprise Offices, Kilkenny Design Centre, high street ranges, fashion weeks and blogs.

notes.b: The Irish clothing and textile industries face strong pressures. Most of them come from competition on price and from the small size of the home market.
points: Imports made in low-wage countries with cheaper and faster labour mean Irish producers find it hard to compete on price.
Discount stores sell clothing at low prices in high volumes, which pressures Irish firms that make smaller runs of higher-quality garments.
The industry is labour-intensive (it needs many workers), so high labour costs for skilled workers push up the price of Irish goods.
A global recession leaves people with less disposable income to spend on clothes.
A small home market limits the number of customers available to Irish designers, so growth depends on export sales.
Firms must adapt to new shopping patterns such as online and mobile shopping, and keep up with trends and technology.
Small firms and cottage industries have limited funds for marketing, equipment and expansion.
A shortage of skilled workers means that keeping them and training new ones is a continuing challenge for manufacturers.
notes.tip: When asked to discuss challenges, give imports and cheap labour abroad, recession and reduced spending, high labour costs, online and mobile shopping, the small home market and skill shortages. Keep to challenges for the industry, not causes of changes in fashion.

notes.h: Careers in the clothing and textile industries
notes.b: The industries offer jobs for creative, technical, presentation and retail talents. Exams ask you to name one career and give details of it, so know what each person does.
points: Creative careers include fashion designer (creates the range), milliner (makes hats), stylist and fashion journalist or writer.
Technical careers include tailor, machinist (sews garments in a factory), clothing manufacturer, factory worker and fashion buyer.
Presentation careers include model and photographer, and fashion advertising and blogging.
Retail careers include retail sales assistant.
To answer a career question, name one career and give two details, such as what the person does, the skills or qualities needed, where they work, and the training route.
notes.tip: Name one career and give two details about it. A list of jobs without detail will not earn full marks on a longer question.

questions.prompt: Explain the role played by small businesses and cottage industries in the Irish clothing industry.
questions.model: Small businesses and cottage industries need little start-up investment, so they allow people to set up in business without large premises or machinery. They provide work in rural areas, which helps keep people in their communities, and they can work around family commitments. They also keep traditional Irish crafts such as knitting, weaving and lace-making alive, and they produce distinctive hand-made products that stand out from mass-produced clothing.

questions.prompt: Discuss the challenges facing the clothing and textile industry in Ireland and outline one way the industry is promoted at home and abroad.
questions.model: Challenges: low-cost manufacturing overseas offers cheaper and faster labour, so Irish producers struggle to compete on price; discount stores sell at low prices in high volumes, which pressures firms making smaller runs of higher-quality garments; the small home market limits customers, so growth depends on exporting; and small firms have limited funds for marketing, equipment and expansion. Keeping skilled workers and training new ones is an ongoing challenge. Promotion: Irish designers show collections at international fashion shows and fashion weeks, and public figures who wear Irish designers' clothing create publicity. Design centres such as Kilkenny Design Centre and the design centre at Powerscourt Townhouse, Dublin, sell the work of Irish designers, and Enterprise Boards support small designers and makers.
